name: Shared State vs Message Passing
question: How do agents know what the others found?
summary: Agents coordinate in one of two ways. They write to a common store, such as a blackboard, scratchpad or typed graph state, or they send each other structured messages. The design choices are who writes which fields, how concurrent writes merge, how much each agent reads, and whether every entry records who wrote it and from which source.
useCases: Several agents contributing findings to one decision
Parallel writers that must not overwrite each other
Audited work where every claim needs a source

items.detail: one typed store every agent can read (blackboard)
how updates merge; with none, a key is overwritten
typed messages sent to named recipients
each agent reads only the fields it needs
who wrote each entry and from which source
an open protocol for messages between separate agent systems

steps: Type the state: findings, open questions, decisions
Give every multi-writer field a reducer such as operator.add
Scope reads so each agent loads only what it needs
Record the author and source on every entry
pitfalls: A key with no reducer loses parallel writes
Free-text chat buries findings and drops sources
remember: Type it, reduce it, scope it, source it.
caption: Illustrative: writers produce 4, 3 and 5 findings of about 0.75k tokens each.

code.text: from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
def dispatcher(s: Board):                    # reads findings only
risks = [f for f in s["findings"] if f["agent"] in ("carrier", "weather")]
for name, fn in [("carrier", carrier), ("weather", weather), ("dispatcher", dispatcher)]:
class Msg:                           # the same flow as typed messages
sender: str; to: str; data: dict; source: str

steps.title: Type the state
steps.text: The board is a typed dict with three fields: findings, open questions and the decision. Every finding is an Entry, not free text.

steps.title: Choose a reducer per field
steps.text: findings and questions use operator.add, so parallel updates are appended. decision has one writer, so plain replacement is safe.

steps.title: Fan out parallel writers
steps.text: The carrier and weather agents start together from START and each returns one finding. Without the reducer, LangGraph would reject the two same-step writes with InvalidUpdateError.

steps.title: Scope reads
steps.text: The dispatcher reads only the findings it needs and writes only the decision. Smaller reads mean fewer tokens and less distraction.

steps.title: Record provenance
steps.text: Every entry names the agent that wrote it and its source, so a reviewer can trace the reroute decision back to the carrier API and the IMD bulletin.

steps.title: Contrast with messages
steps.text: The same flow can run as typed messages sent to a named recipient. Each agent then sees only what is addressed to it; protocols such as A2A standardise this across systems.

pros: Parallel findings are merged instead of lost
Typed fields make findings checkable and easy to read
Scoped reads keep each agent’s context small
cons: A missing reducer silently loses writes, or raises errors
A shared board invites everyone to read everything
Message passing needs routing and addressing
avoidWhen: One agent does all the work: its own state is enough
Agents never need each other’s findings

playgroundGuide.scenario: During a festive sale, up to six agents (carrier, warehouse, weather, customs, fleet and returns) assess each at-risk shipment in parallel. They produce 4, 3, 5, 4, 3 and 5 findings of about 0.75k tokens each, and every agent then reads what it needs to decide. The team can share through a typed board, a free-text group chat or typed messages to named agents.
controls: Choose how agents share: a shared board, free-text chat or typed messages.
Set the number of parallel writers and, on the board, the reducer and read scope.
Turn agent and source fields on every entry on or off.

outputs.meaning: Findings overwritten or buried and never picked up.

outputs.meaning: What one agent loads, against reading every finding once.

outputs.meaning: Entries that record which agent wrote them and from which source.

presets.name: Board, no reducer
presets.expect: 3 writers with no reducer: only the last writer’s 5 findings survive, so 7 of 12 are lost, with 2 colliding writes. Reads look small (3.8k against 9k) only because data is missing. Provenance 50%.

presets.name: Append reducer
presets.expect: 4 writers with operator.add: nothing lost of 16, but every agent reads all 12k tokens. Provenance 50%.

presets.name: Free-text chat
presets.expect: 4 writers in a group chat: nothing is overwritten, but about 3 findings are buried, everyone reads 19.2k tokens of prose, 2 contradictions stay open, provenance 30%.

presets.name: Typed messages
presets.expect: 3 writers sending typed messages: nothing lost, each agent reads 6k against 9k, provenance 60% because sources are not recorded.

missions.text: Lose 0 findings with 4 or more parallel writers.
missions.hint: Use the append reducer on the board, or typed messages.

missions.text: Without losing anything, halve the tokens each agent reads compared with reading every finding.
missions.hint: With 4 or more writers, scope reads to the fields each agent needs, or use typed messages.
Turn on agent and source fields.

tools.best: Explicit graphs with typed state, reducers, parallel branches, checkpoints and interrupts.
tools.ex: Carrier, warehouse and weather nodes write to one typed board that a dispatcher node reads.
pros: Precise control of state and flow

tools.best: Role agents that publish structured documents to a shared message pool and subscribe by role.
tools.ex: A product manager agent publishes a requirements document that engineer agents subscribe to.
pros: Publish-subscribe cuts what each role reads
cons: Less general than a graph library

tools.best: Messages, tasks and artefacts between separately built agent systems, discovered through Agent Cards.
tools.ex: A bank’s KYC agent sends a task to a vendor’s document-verification agent and receives an artefact back.

tools.best: Studying an orchestrator that keeps a shared task ledger and progress ledger for its team.
tools.ex: Read how the ledgers record facts, guesses and the plan, then compare with a typed board.
cons: Built on AutoGen, now in maintenance mode
A research system, not a product

tools.best: Passing selected earlier task outputs as context to later tasks in a crew.
tools.ex: A pricing task receives only the competitor-research task’s output as context.
pros: Simple scoping of what each task sees

practice.scenario: During a festive sale, a Bengaluru e-commerce logistics team runs three agents per at-risk shipment: carrier, warehouse and weather. All three write findings, each with its source, to one typed shipment-risk board. A dispatcher agent reads the board and decides whether to reroute, and parallel writes are merged with an append reducer so nothing is lost.

industries.use: Carrier, warehouse and weather agents write to one shipment-risk board
Document, fraud and coverage agents share a typed claim file
Log, metrics and deploy agents post findings to one incident record

practice.analogy: A hospital patient chart. Each specialist adds dated, signed notes to the same chart; nobody erases another’s entry, and each reads only the sections they need.

library.name: LangGraph
library.what: Graph state is a typed dict; a reducer per key decides how updates merge, and parallel branches join before the next node runs.

practice.note: In LangGraph, two parallel nodes writing the same key with no reducer raise InvalidUpdateError; sequential writes simply overwrite.

numericDrill.question: Four agents each write 5 findings of 0.6k tokens to a shared board, and each agent then reads the board. How many tokens (in thousands) does each agent read if it reads everything?
numericDrill.answer: 4 × 5 = 20 findings × 0.6k = 12k tokens per agent. If each reads only the 2 fields it needs (say a quarter of the board), that falls to 3k.

interview.question: What happens in LangGraph when two parallel nodes write the same key?
interview.answer: If the key has no reducer, LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError because it cannot pick one value; sequential writes simply overwrite. With a reducer such as operator.add, the updates are merged.

interview.question: When would you choose message passing over a shared board?
interview.answer: When agents belong to separate systems or teams, when each should see only what is addressed to it, or when you need an auditable record of who told whom what. Protocols such as A2A standardise those messages across systems.

mistakes.mistake: Don’t leave a multi-writer field without a reducer.
mistakes.fix: Declare how updates merge, for example Annotated[list, operator.add].

mistakes.mistake: Don’t let every agent read everything.
mistakes.fix: Scope reads to the fields each agent needs, and record the author and source of every entry.

quiz.question: Three parallel LangGraph nodes each return {"findings": [x]} into a key declared as findings: list[str]. What happens?
options: LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError, because the key has no reducer and receives several values in one step
Only the first write is kept
quiz.explanation: Without a reducer LangGraph cannot choose between concurrent values for one key, so it rejects the update.

quiz.question: How do you fix that board so all three findings are kept?
options: Run the nodes one after another
Rename the key in each node
quiz.explanation: operator.add is a reducer that concatenates the updates, so parallel writes merge.

quiz.question: A claim file is shared by several agents. Which fields need a reducer? Select all that apply.
options: Findings written by the document, fraud and coverage agents
Open questions that any agent may add
The final decision, written only by the adjudicator
The claim ID, set once at the start
quiz.explanation: Fields with several writers need a merge rule. Single-writer or write-once fields can use plain replacement.

quiz.question: Five agents each write 6 findings of about 0.5k tokens, and every agent then reads the whole board. How many tokens do the five agents read in total?
quiz.explanation: The board holds 5 × 6 × 0.5k = 15k tokens; five agents each read it: 5 × 15k = 75k.

quiz.question: On the same board, each agent reads only the findings of the 2 writers it depends on. How many tokens do the five agents read in total?
quiz.explanation: Each reads 2 × 6 × 0.5k = 6k; five agents: 5 × 6k = 30k.

quiz.question: An AML team asks every agent to record its name and source on each finding. What does this buy?
options: An audit trail: every statement in the note can be traced to who wrote it and where it came from
quiz.explanation: Provenance makes findings auditable, which regulators and analysts need.

quiz.question: Agents coordinate through a free-text group chat. What problems are likely? Select all that apply.
options: Findings are buried in prose and missed
Parallel writes are rejected with an error
quiz.explanation: Free text keeps every message but buries findings, loses sources and makes everyone read everything. Rejected writes are a typed-state problem.

quiz.question: A bank’s KYC agent must discover what a vendor’s document-verification agent can do before sending it work over A2A. What does it read?
quiz.explanation: In A2A, an Agent Card advertises an agent’s identity, capabilities and how to reach it.

quiz.question: In MetaGPT, how do role agents share work?
options: Each role reads every chat message
Roles publish structured documents to a shared message pool and subscribe to what their role needs
Roles hand off the conversation one by one
quiz.explanation: MetaGPT uses a shared message pool with publish–subscribe by role, which scopes what each agent reads.

quiz.question: A board replaces the findings list on every write. Three parallel writers produce 6, 4 and 5 findings, and the writer with 5 finishes last. How many findings are lost?
quiz.explanation: Only the last write survives: 5 of 15 kept, so 10 are lost.

quiz.question: When is typed message passing a better fit than a shared board? Select all that apply.
options: The agents belong to different organisations or systems
You need a record of who sent what to whom
All agents live in one graph and feed one decision
Only one agent does all the work
quiz.explanation: Messages suit separate systems and auditable exchanges. One graph feeding one decision is the board’s home ground; one agent needs neither.

quiz.question: In LangGraph, a node updates a key that has no reducer, and no other node writes it in that step. What happens to the old value?
options: It is kept and the update ignored
quiz.explanation: The default for a key without a reducer is to overwrite it with the new value.

quiz.question: A chat app’s LangGraph state uses add_messages for its messages key. What does that reducer do?
options: Merges new messages into the list, updating any with the same ID
quiz.explanation: add_messages appends new messages and updates existing ones that share an ID.

quiz.question: A claim file has 60 entries, and 48 of them name both the agent and the source. What is the provenance rate?
What did the 2025 blackboard multi-agent paper (Han et al.) report against static and dynamic multi-agent baselines?
options: The best average performance while spending fewer tokens
Higher accuracy at triple the tokens
quiz.explanation: The authors report the best average performance across their datasets with fewer tokens than the baselines.

quiz.question: A research team’s board holds prices, news, filings and analyst notes. Which read rules scope reads well? Select all that apply.
options: The valuation agent reads only prices and filings
Each agent reads only the fields it needs
Every agent reads the full board to be safe
Writers re-read their own output on every step
quiz.explanation: Scoped reads cut tokens and distraction. Reading everything, or re-reading one’s own output, wastes context.

quiz.question: What role does Magentic-One’s task ledger play?
options: It is a shared record of facts, guesses and the plan that the orchestrator keeps up to date
quiz.explanation: The task ledger is an explicit shared record that the orchestrator uses to plan and replan.

quiz.question: The carrier agent reports an ETA of Friday; the warehouse agent reports Saturday. How should the board handle it?
options: Keep both, each with its agent, source and time, and resolve them by a stated rule or escalate
quiz.explanation: With provenance on both entries, a rule (for example, trust the carrier’s scan data) or a person can resolve the conflict transparently.

quiz.question: An incident board records findings from log, metrics and deploy agents. Which fields should each entry carry? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Author, source and time make entries traceable and orderable. The system prompt adds tokens without helping anyone audit the finding.

quiz.question: A board holds 40 findings of 0.8k tokens. The dispatcher’s read scope covers 25% of them. How many tokens does it read?
